Commentary.Commentary: So, that’s how things ended here in Canberra - a promising contest turned into a soggy disappointment. Now, the focus shifts to Melbourne, where the second T20I will take place on Friday, 31st October. The first ball is scheduled to be bowled at 1.45 pm IST (8.15 am GMT), and both teams will be desperate to get a full game in, though there is rain predicted in Melbourne as well. As this series has now lasted for four matches, expect India to carry their batting flair forward, and Australia to come back stronger with the ball. The stage will be bigger, the crowd louder, and hopefully the skies clearer. Join us an hour early for all the pre-match build-up and insights. Until then, breathe and smile! TAKE CARE! CIAO!

Earlier,  Mitchell Marsh won the toss and decided to bowl first. India’s openers came out firing, with Abhishek Sharma striking a few sweet boundaries before Ellis drew first blood. Then came the drizzle. Covers on. Frustration up. After a brief delay, the match was trimmed to 18 overs per side, and India restarted with intent. Suryakumar Yadav and Shubman Gill showed why they’re the talk of the town. SKY’s classy flicks and Gill’s effortless timing pushed India to 97/1 in just 9.4 overs before… yep, the rain returned. Hazlewood bowled tightly but couldn’t find a breakthrough, while Ellis was the only one with a scalp to his name. In total, we got just more than nine overs of play and two lengthy interruptions.

UPDATE - 4.36 pm IST (11.06 am GMT) - Unfortunately, we won't have any cricket further this evening as the MATCH HAS BEEN CALLED OFF. Steady rain wins in Canberra. The players shake hands with a smile, hiding their frustration, because, well, what else can you do when the skies just won’t stop crying? The crowd waited, the covers came on and off, but eventually, nature had its final say. It is a shame, as we were so well set for a cracker of a game.

UPDATE - 4.22 pm IST (10.52 am GMT) - Latest word suggests 4.50 pm IST (11.20 am GMT) marks the absolute deadline for resumption, which would leave Australia chasing a DLS-adjusted target of 71 from 5 overs. That scenario hinges entirely on the rain relenting completely, and time is rapidly slipping away.

It's a busy cricketing Wednesday as there are a couple of more matches lined up on the roster for the day. The second T20I between Bangladesh and West Indies is set to commence shortly in Chattogram, with the Caribbean visitors holding a 1-0 advantage in the three-match series. Meanwhile, Afghanistan's tour of Zimbabwe sees the opening T20I of their three-match leg also starting shortly in Harare.

UPDATE - 4 pm IST (10.30 am GMT) - Okay, scratch the previous update as the rain has picked up again and it is pelting down steadily. Looks like we are in for a long delay. Bear in mind, we've got roughly an hour and a half remaining to complete this match. It seemingly appears India's innings is done, and we will jump straight into Australia's chase upon resumption. Nothing official yet, but that outcome looks unavoidable at this stage.

As we wait for the rain to relent in Canberra, let us brief you all on what's happening in Guwahati. In the first semifinal of the ICC Women's Cricket World Cup 2025, England Women have opted to bowl first against South Africa Women at the Barsapara Cricket Stadium. The Proteas have gotten off to a very positive start through Laura Wolvaardt and Tazmin Brits. The winner of this crucial match will qualify for the finale, while the loser will pack up and fly back home. You can follow all the live action from that game by hopping into the other tab.

UPDATE - 3.47 pm IST (10.17 am GMT) - Still raining, but it looks like the intensity has slowed down a bit. Let's hope that it stops completely as quickly as possible. However, given the amount of water taken by the outfield already, it will surely take a bit more time to prepare the ground for resumption. Fingers crossed. Stay tuned for further updates.

UPDATE - 3.27 pm IST (9.57 am GMT) - Well, well, guess who's back? It has started to rain again in Canberra and the players are requested to go off the field. Suryakumar Yadav cradles his bat under his jersey as he walks off. It is getting heavier as we speak. Ugh! It's frustrating. Australia won't mind this stoppage, as the Indians were going all guns blazing after the resumption. But for sure, this contest will be further truncated when we resume again.

UPDATE - We are hearing that NITISH KUMAR REDDY has been RULED OUT of the first 3 T20Is. He suffered a strain in his left quadriceps in the ODI series, and he is still recovering from that injury.

India (Playing XI) - Abhishek Sharma, Shubman Gill, Tilak Varma, Suryakumar Yadav (C), Sanju Samson (WK), Shivam Dube, Axar Patel, Harshit Rana, Kuldeep Yadav, Varun Chakaravarthy, and Jasprit Bumrah.

Australia (Playing XI) - Mitchell Marsh (C), Travis Head, Josh Inglis (WK), Tim David, Mitchell Owen, Marcus Stoinis, Josh Philippe, Xavier Bartlett, Nathan Ellis, Matthew Kuhnemann, and Josh Hazlewood.

The captain of India, Suryakumar Yadav, expresses that they were looking to bat first, so they got what they wanted. He says that it looks like a good wicket and reckons that it might get a bit slower as the game goes on. Mentions their analyst highlighted the limited amount of cricket played at this venue. Says the guys know exactly what needs to be done and know their roles very well. Informs that the guys missing out are Rinku Singh, Washington Sundar, Arshdeep Singh, Jitesh Sharma, and Nitish Kumar Reddy.

The skipper of Australia, Mitchell Marsh, says that they will bowl first. He feels that it looks like a really good wicket and mentions that it usually plays well here. Adds that the team has been playing good, aggressive cricket lately and expects India to do the same, calling them the number one side in the world. Marsh says that it’s going to be an exciting contest between two power-packed teams, both pushing hard with the World Cup around the corner. With a cheeky grin, he also informs that they’re playing with eleven players - a few batters, a few bowlers, and some all-rounders, keeping the mood light before the big clash.

TOSS - It's TOSS time in the Australian capital... and yes, you absolutely read that in Ravi Shastri's voice. A chilly evening greets proceedings as both skippers stride out, sweaters layered over their jerseys to combat the cold. The flip of the coin is won by Australia and Mitchell Marsh elects to BOWL first.

PITCH REPORT - Former Indian keeper-batter, Parthiv Patel, is down at the center with his assessment. Speaking about the conditions, he notes that it’s cool and slightly overcast, which could make things interesting early on. Points out that there’s a good grass cover on the surface, which means the seamers will get some early assistance with a hint of lateral movement on offer. However, Parthiv adds that once the ball gets a bit older, batters will enjoy the pace and bounce, as it should come nicely onto the bat. Mentions that dew might play a role later in the evening, which could make defending tricky. Overall, he concludes that it looks like a fine surface for batting, but early discipline with the ball will be key for the pacers to make an impact.

Let's hear from India's Sanju Samson, who had a quick chat with the broadcasters a bit earlier. He begins by saying that it feels good to come out of the Kerala heat and enjoy some cold weather in Canberra. Mentions the team held a meeting the other day, where they discussed the significance of the three upcoming T20I series ahead of the World Cup. States that the focus remains on taking things match by match and testing themselves under pressure against Australia. Adds that the conditions here will be quite challenging as well. Regarding his team role, he acknowledges he's fulfilled various roles across different teams and is prepared to embrace whatever's required. He further notes he's opened the batting, closed out games as a finisher, and is now slotted into the middle order. Adds that beyond the openers, every batter must be prepared to walk in at any moment under any circumstances, and the team has trained extensively for precisely that flexibility. Ends by saying that he is looking forward to doing both batting and wicket-keeping.

Manuka Oval's T20I sample size remains limited, but the existing data tells a clear story. The first innings average score is in the range of 145-150, suggesting the surface offers genuine assistance to bowlers. The win-loss split sits perfectly balanced at 2-2 between batting and chasing sides. But notably, pursuing targets beyond 150 has historically proven troublesome here. Weather concerns? Rain lashed Canberra earlier, but the forecast suggests minimal interruption during match hours. It is pretty overcast at the moment, but a full contest looks almost assured. Stay locked in as toss and teams will flash shortly on your screens.

From the Indian camp, the return of Jasprit Bumrah after missing out on the ODI series is a major headline, while Nitish Kumar Reddy’s inclusion at the expense of injured Hardik Pandya is the only major change in the Indian squad. India's equally strong spell includes their unbeaten run through the Asia Cup, with their last defeat coming at home to England earlier this year. The statistics grow more remarkable when zoomed out. India haven't lost a T20I bilateral series on Australian soil since 2008, a streak they'll be desperate to preserve. Since 2022, just one series defeat and one draw have punctuated an otherwise flawless run in the format. Now, as India's next generation touches Down Under in Suryakumar Yadav's leadership, the challenge becomes sustaining these towering legacies.

Australia, to their credit, are playing top-quality cricket in the shortest format lately. They haven’t lost a series in this calendar year, and will be chasing their fifth consecutive series win as well. Mitchell Marsh continues to lead the side, though with several key personnel diverted to Ashes preparations, the squad will circle around significant reshuffling and reinforcements as the series goes on. But still, it maintains the feature of a luxury in batting and bowling depth. The batting order, more or less, is the same, and of course, menacing. But Matthew Short’s injury recovery opens the door for Josh Philippe for the keeper-batter role, though the first choice is likely Josh Inglis, with Ben McDermott called in as extra cover. It is the bowling unit that is equally threatening too. Josh Hazlewood leads the pack, including a streak of proven pacers in this format.

Although the upcoming Ashes can be rightfully called the Australian summer’s grandest spectacle, this series, too, holds an equal importance between two arch-rivals, who have treated fans with some really competitive games, justifying the word ‘rivalry’ in a true sense. You don’t often see an international fixture scheduled in Canberra, as this is just the sixth T20I at this venue, and the first match in this format after three long years. So, it is indeed a special occasion. Australia hold a so-so record at Manuka Oval with an equal distribution of wins and defeats, 2-2. While India have played just once here, way back in 2020, and have emerged victorious.

Around four months and a handful of days remain for the upcoming T20 World Cup, and the dress rehearsals are about to intensify with Australia hosting a power-packed 5-match T20I series against the defending champions, India. The number 1 team faces the team ranked second in the shortest format after a thrilling ODI series, which was bagged by the Aussies. It all begins at the Australian capital city of Canberra with the beautiful setting of the Manuka Oval. On that note, we extend our warm welcome to everyone joining us for the coverage. Always a pleasure to have you all with us.
... MATCH DAY ...

The sun never sets on cricket’s drama, as it only changes its stage. And that glowing stage moves to Canberra, where India and Australia are set to light up the first T20I at the Manuka Oval of this blockbuster 5-match series. The white-ball rivalry between India and Australia has been fierce all these years, and this time again, it’s more than just another series - it’s the dress rehearsal for the upcoming T20I World Cup 2026. After Australia’s 2-1 dominance in the ODIs, the caravan moves to the shorter, louder, and more unpredictable format. The air feels different now - fresher, faster, and filled with hope. Both teams know that this T20I series isn’t about bragging rights - it’s about fine-tuning for the biggest stage to come next year. Momentum, confidence, and combinations - all will be tested in these fiery nights Down Under. What a build-up it has been! The ODI leg showed the contrast between the two sides - Australia’s discipline versus India’s flashes of brilliance that faded too soon. The Aussies, with their mix of experience and youth, showed why they’re masters at home, while India looked like a team searching for rhythm and identity. Now, as the focus shifts to the T20Is, the equation changes. Shorter format, bigger risks, and even louder roars - this is where the brave flourish and the uncertain fade. Can India turn the tide? Or will Australia’s juggernaut roll on? For India, this T20I series is the perfect chance to reset the tone. Led by Suryakumar Yadav, they’ve brought in a fresh, hungry, and daring group - one that screams intent and entertainment. Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma, Rinku Singh, and vice-captain Shubman Gill headline the next-gen batting order that has lit up recent tournaments. The bowling pack, too, looks sharp - Bumrah brings experience, Arshdeep brings swing, and Kuldeep Yadav brings magic. The big goal? To fix the death overs, find a stable finisher, and prepare a team that can own 2026. The absence of veterans like Rohit and Kohli in T20Is now adds an emotional layer, but the baton is officially passed, though their shadows still inspire every young batter in blue. Australia, meanwhile, enter this series on a high, and how could they not? They dominated the ODIs with skill, flair, and adaptability. But in T20Is, they face a different kind of challenge - quick thinking, rotating roles, and finding the right mix ahead of the next T20I World Cup. Mitchell Marsh will once again lead, and the team news has been a bit fizzing - Adam Zampa will miss the start of the series, replaced by young leggie Tanveer Sangha. Glenn Maxwell returns from a wrist injury, Mahli Beardman earns a surprise debut call, and Travis Head looks to continue his golden touch. This team is deep, dangerous, and, more importantly, determined to keep their home record shining. The Aussies’ biggest strength lies in their balance - Marsh, Head, Short, and David bring firepower, while Hazlewood ensures discipline with the new ball. Their weakness? Perhaps the over-reliance on power-hitting when the pitch doesn’t suit it, and the spin department without Zampa, looks slightly inexperienced. But when Australia play at home, they almost always find a way to dominate - their energy, confidence, and crowd support create an aura that’s hard to crack. India will need every ounce of courage to push through that storm. Both teams come with unfinished business and a hunger that can be felt even before a ball is bowled. For India, it’s about proving that the new generation can carry the same fire that once defined their greats. For Australia, it’s about showing that their dominance isn’t limited to formats or conditions. Every player knows these games matter - not just for reputations, but for the places in the World Cup squad, and for pride that runs deep in every jersey. The pitch at the Manuka Oval promises a fair contest - good bounce, some movement early on, and runs galore if you survive the new ball. The evening breeze could help seamers like Hazlewood and Bumrah, while spinners such as Kuldeep and Sangha might find grip in the middle overs. Bat first or chase? That eternal T20 dilemma! But one thing’s certain - fans can expect sixes flying, wickets tumbling, and drama unfolding under the lights. And what about those key battles? Bumrah versus Head is the chess match of pace and instinct. Abhishek Sharma against Hazlewood’s precision could define India’s starts. Kuldeep Yadav spinning his web around Matthew Short might decide the middle overs. And then, the fireworks - Suryakumar Yadav versus Australia’s death bowlers. Whoever wins those mini-duels could very well win the game itself. On paper, Australia hold the edge - they’re home, confident, and already leading India’s tour. But India, with their youthful zeal and nothing-to-lose attitude, can be unpredictable - dangerously so. If their top order fires and Bumrah does what he does best, this could turn into a thrilling fightback story. One thing’s for sure, when these two giants collide under the Canberra sky, cricket will sing its most beautiful chaos once again!
